#187. Man arrested in Nashville after DNA links him to unsolved 1990s rape cases

Archibald Amory, 58, reportedly being held in Tennessee pending return to New York, where he was tied to two cases

A man has been arrested in Nashville after DNA linked him to a series of unsolved New York City rapes from the 1990s, according to a news report.

Archibald Amory, 58, was detained on Thursday in Hermitage, a neighborhood of Nashville, and is being held there pending his return to New York City, according to the Daily News, citing sources and Nashville authorities.

Amory has been linked via DNA to two rapes that took place in Queens, and connected to several other uncharged sex assaults. Sources said recent advances in DNA technology and investigative methods helped identify Amory.

Court papers filed in Tennessee said special victims investigators in Nashville and with the NYPD “identified Archibald Amory as a wanted fugitive in connection to a series of rape investigations originating in the jurisdiction of New York City”.

Armory appeared in court in Nashville on Monday, according to a spokesperson for the district attorney of Davidson county. He is currently being held on $800,000 bond.

Another man has also been arrested, in Miami, for allegedly raping a woman in New York’s Central Park last month.

Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, was arrested on Tuesday at a Miami Burger King where he had been working. Police said he will also be charged in two other Central Park rapes.

Rivera-Deleon will be charged with the sexual assault of a 39-year-old woman who was walking just outside Central Park on 24 October when he pulled a knife on her near E 66th Street and Fifth Avenue.

The suspect allegedly dragged the victim into the park, where he raped her, before a bystander, who witnessed the attack, called 911. Rivera-Deleon was identified as the attacker via surveillance film, and investigators have linked him to a Central Park rape in 2023 and another in 2021.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

#186. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#184. Trump’s ‘trade deal’ with Thailand is not a done deal.

The next stop on President Trump’s whirlwind Asia trip is the city of Shenzhen, where he is expected to meet with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

Follow live updates on President Trump’s trip to Asia.

President Trump met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday ahead of a flight to the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where he was expected to cap his whirlwind visit to Asia by meeting the leaders of China and Russia.

Mr. Marcos gave Mr. Trump a red-carpet welcome at the Malacañang Palace, complete with a military guard and a gun salute ahead of a bilateral meeting and banquet lunch. The U.S. delegation included Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

In his remarks to Mr. Marcos, Mr. Trump described the U.S.-Philippine relationship as “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific.”

Mr. Trump was expected to leave right after, having spent less than 24 hours in the Philippine capital. He briefly attended a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders and also met with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India on Tuesday.

In Shenzhen, the president is expected to attend the APEC economic summit, followed by a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. Mr. Trump’s unpredictable agenda could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.

The brief itinerary in Asia appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.

Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. The only event of substance on his schedule for the day — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

Mr. Trump also met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.

In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.

Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.

Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.

North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.

Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.

Palace history: Mr. Marcos hosted Mr. Trump at Malacañang Palace, where the Philippine leader spent much of his childhood. He left the palace in military fatigues 40 years ago when his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, was ousted. Read more ›

In remarks at lunch, Trump spoke of the long history between the United States and the Philippines and noted that Gen. Douglas MacArthur had once received a gold baton in the Malacañang Palace. The honor was presented to MacArthur in 1936 when he was appointed field marshal of the Philippines by President Manuel L. Quezon.

“I’d love that,” Trump joked. “I mean, why the hell shouldn’t I get that?”

At a lunch with Marcos, Trump said that the United States and the Philippines had just signed a trade deal, without giving more details.

“We didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both,” he said.

Xi has begun talks with Putin in Shenzhen, according to Chinese state media. The two leaders were expected to meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit ahead of a trilateral summit with Trump.

In his remarks to Marcos, Trump said the U.S.-Philippine relationship was “one of America’s oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific,” adding that the Philippines was a key pillar of security in the region.

“Our alliance has never been better,” Trump said.

Trump, while describing his administration’s support of arms sales to the Philippines, took a moment to praise the U.S. military’s efforts in Iran. “We’re doing very well in Iran, to put it mildly,” he said.

Seated next to Marcos at the meeting with Trump was the Philippine foreign affairs secretary, Maria Theresa Lazaro, the only high-ranking woman official in sight during days of high-level political meetings.

While Trump and Marcos met in Manila, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia was speaking to business leaders in Shenzhen, China, at the APEC CEO summit. Putin said his coming meeting with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping had “great potential benefits.”

Marcos said the two sides would not be signing an agreement on the Pax Silica artificial intelligence supply chain initiative today. The American-led initiative, an effort to build a China-free supply chain for the A.I. industry, has been met with resistance in the Philippines.

In his opening remarks, Trump hailed potential collaboration with the Philippines in the energy sector, noting that the United States is the world’s leading producer of oil and natural gas. He said that oil reserves in Venezuela, which he described as “our new acquisition,” and a new pipeline in Alaska would enable the United States to provide affordable, abundant energy supplies to its allies.

As their meeting began, Marcos said he had fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee delivered as a late-night snack for Trump on Tuesday.

“It’s providing extra energy for all the work that is in front of you,” Marcos said to Trump.

Malacañang Palace was once the home of an American president, William Howard Taft, who moved into the riverside property in 1901 as governor-general of the Philippines.

Trump signed a guest book at the palace, writing, “This is such a great honor. The U.S.A. loves you!”

The presidential palace is all decked out in Christmas décor. It may be early, but the Philippines starts preparing for the holiday as early as September.

Stephen Miller, the president’s new chief of staff, was in the lineup at the arrival ceremony, as was Dan Scavino, the White House deputy chief of staff. Howard Lutnick and Scott Bessent, two officials who have been feuding over the administration’s approach to exporting Nvidia technology, were also there, and stood next to each other. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, was also in the lineup.

President Trump was received on Wednesday by his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., at Malacañang Palace in Manila, where Mr. Marcos spent much of his childhood.

Forty years ago, he left the compound in military fatigues, when his family fled into exile after a popular uprising ousted his father, the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.

Mr. Trump received a red-carpet welcome with full military honors at the palace, which sits by the Pasig River. The lavish compound was originally built as a summer house for a Spanish aristocrat until the colonial government, which ruled the Philippines for over 300 years, bought it in 1825 and converted it into a seat of power for the governor general.

It had been the younger Marcos’s home since he was seven years old. It was where he saw state leaders meeting with his father, and he has recalled needing to be dressed properly at all times.

The family moved there after the elder Mr. Marcos was elected president in 1965. They stayed for nearly two decades, with much of that time during the authoritarian rule of Mr. Marcos, who declared martial law.

The younger Mr. Marcos returned to the grounds as a resident after he was elected president in 2022. “It’s almost funny, my return to the palace, it feels ordinary because I lived there for so long,” he said at the time. “But when you think about it carefully, it really isn’t ordinary, because I came back to the place, I’ve become president, and even if what I’m doing is the same, it feels different.”

What he liked most about the palace was being spoiled as a child. “You were very attended to. You were very well cared for,” he said.

On Feb. 25, 1986, the younger Marcos, then 28, was photographed standing beside his father on a palace balcony as the latter delivered a speech claiming he had won another term. That same night, the Marcoses fled to Hawaii on board American helicopters.

On previous international trips, the American delegation has included Trump’s former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and Karoline Leavitt, his former press secretary. The departure of several top-ranking women within the Trump administration has led to a notable, male-only lineup of U.S. officials who assembled to greet the Philippine president.

Trump was dressed in a suit and red tie while Marcos wore a traditional barong shirt.

Trump was greeted by a military guard outside the palace. He saluted as he stood next to Marcos in front of a row of American and Philippine flags, while a band played the national anthems of both countries.

Protesters are marching toward the presidential palace in Manila, where hundreds of riot police officers have been deployed to head off any trouble. Many of the protesters are university students, who joined the protests during the week-long holiday break announced by the government to coincide with the ASEAN summit.

President Trump is on his way to meet President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines at his official residence, the Malacañang Palace in Manila. The Philippines is the United States’ oldest treaty ally in Asia, but there is public unease about U.S. artificial intelligence projects in the country as well as questions about Washington’s reliability as a partner.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.

Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.

Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.

As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.

A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.

On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.

Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”

Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.

During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines:  “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”

It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos, who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.

The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.

During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”

India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.

President Trump is expected to meet with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul of Thailand on Tuesday in Manila to sign what the White House has described as a “trade deal.”

But Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Tuesday that Bangkok was expecting to agree only on a “joint statement marking progress in negotiations.”

The dissonance comes amid growing signs within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. The meeting between Mr. Trump and Mr. Anutin is taking place on the sidelines of an ASEAN summit.

For more than a year, Washington and Bangkok have been negotiating a new trade agreement that covers items like tariffs, food imports and labor rights.

Last year, the United States battered Thailand with a 36 percent tariff, one of the steepest rates levied by Mr. Trump after his return to office. The United States is one of Thailand’s largest export markets, including for goods like pet food.

Mr. Trump later reduced the tariffs to 19 percent, before the U.S. Supreme Court struck them down in February. The administration eventually found a way to still impose 12.5 percent tariffs on Thai goods.

The signing of a U.S.-Thai trade deal might still be far off, requiring Thailand’s parliament to pass a law, but the meeting delivers an easy publicity win for Mr. Anutin and Mr. Trump, who is known to revel even in perceived success.

Pavida Pananond, an economist at Thammasat Business School in Bangkok, said, “The level of trust Thailand has in the U.S. is not at the same level as before all this economic weaponization of tariffs.”

Several hundred activists massed on Tuesday in central Manila to march to the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

By the time President Trump landed in the city, the ranks of the protesters had swelled to thousands.

Most of the demonstrators were university students who said that they were fed up with the government, which they said was more focused on preserving its relationship with the United States than helping impoverished Filipinos.

Cinna Sison, 18, who studies European languages at the University of the Philippines, said they were inspired by the recent mass protests in France.

“I love the French,” she said. “They know how to protest.”

Ms. Sison said she had worn colorful makeup to mark her first time attending a demonstration. “I am here to show my solidarity with fellow young activists. We are here to show our disgust to the fascist Trump and to Marcos for kowtowing to his every wish,” she said, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines.

Mr. Trump is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Mr. Marcos on Wednesday before he heads to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

The Philippine president, who earlier this year described Washington as a “steadfast partner,” has said little publicly about meeting Mr. Trump. His administration has hinted that the two sides are working on a military aid agreement.

In Manila, Ms. Sison wore a red scarf on her head and a red shirt with the words “Silicone not Silica” — a reference to Pax Silica, a U.S.-led consortium of countries aiming to create artificial intelligence supply chains independent of China.

Ms. Sison added that Pax Silica was a symbolic return of the Americans to the Philippines, the site of former U.S. military bases, as Washington leaned on a regional ally to counter China.

“Neighborliness is important, but it is not important to be subservient to U.S. interests,” she said.

Nearby, Raja Bausing, a 22-year-old visual artist, was busy putting the finishing touches on a papier-mâché model of Mr. Trump holding Mr. Marcos.

“We want to show how Trump is a warmonger, while Marcos is a lap dog,” she said. “They are very disrespectful to Filipinos. Trump was welcomed in a grand way and yet we Filipinos are maltreated.”

President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday, beginning a trip to Asia in which he will attend an ASEAN summit, greet members of the Quad, then travel to China for an APEC meeting.

Here’s what those acronyms mean, as well as some highlights from previous summits — including gold crowns and awkward handshakes.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum is a group of 21 member economies, most of which are from that region. Its members also include Canada, Mexico, Australia, Russia and the United States. It promotes trade in Asia, but is not a free trade bloc. Its leaders meet annually, with the location rotating each year.

Meetings between world leaders on the sidelines of the summit can often overshadow the main proceedings. This year, in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, Mr. Trump is expected to meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, as well as with Mr. Xi separately.

Last year, when Mr. Trump visited the South Korean city of Gyeongju during the week of the APEC meeting, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea gave him a replica of a gold crown that researchers believe was worn by an ancient Korean ruler. Mr. Trump also met with Mr. Xi in the nearby city of Busan, where the two struck a truce in their countries’ trade war.

A notable incident happened in Sydney, Australia, in 2007, when a group of local television comedians brought an Osama bin Laden look-alike through security. The team came within yards of a hotel where President George W. Bush was staying.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations is a grouping of 11 countries — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, East Timor and Vietnam — which promotes political cooperation and stability across the region. Its leaders meet twice annually.

The bloc was formed in 1967 and represents nearly 700 million people. Its economy and its role in global markets have strengthened in recent years. The United States also sees ASEAN as a geostrategic bulwark against China.

In 2009, an ASEAN meeting in Thailand fell into acrimony when Secretary of State Hillary Clinton compared North Korea’s leaders to “small children” when discussing their nuclear program. The country’s leadership, in turn, described Ms. Clinton as a “schoolgirl” and a “pensioner.”

During the 2017 ASEAN summit in Manila, Mr. Trump grimaced while jostling with Southeast Asian leaders for an awkward cross-armed handshake that was captured in a group photograph.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue is an informal partnership between Australia, India, Japan and the United States, which was formed in part to counter China. It was proposed by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan in 2007.

Beijing opposed the initial discussion, lodging formal diplomatic protests. Australia withdrew in 2008 and the dialogue was put on hold for some time. But the grouping was revived in 2017 on the sidelines of an ASEAN conference.

President Biden was the first U.S. president to convene a meeting among the leaders of the nations as a foursome. In 2024, he hosted the Quad leaders at his home in Wilmington, Del. Mr. Trump has appeared to be less enthusiastic about the partnership. Last year, he did not attend the Quad summit in India.

Reporting from the village of Manabayucan in the Philippines and the capital, Manila

In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that U.S. officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub.

He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica.

Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there?

Months later, he says he has few answers.

“I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.”

The United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence.

Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to Pax Americana, the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II.

The significance of Pax Silica, which 26 signatories have joined, has become heightened after revelations that Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence, exposing the growing geopolitical stakes of the global A.I. race.

In the Philippines, America’s oldest ally in Asia, the backlash has been fierce.

#183. US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race

The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.

The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.

Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.

The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.

"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.

Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.

Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.

Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.

The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.

The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.

"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.

Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.

The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

#181. ‘Plume’ of decomposing garbage, gas prompts emergency health order for LA county residents

Landfill operators have been ordered to provide hotel accommodations and other care to area residents

Officials in a Los Angeles county have ordered the operators of a landfill to provide hotel accommodations and other care to nearby residents after it exploded with decomposing garbage and methane gas.

A noxious, dark geyser of material and smoke began to spew from the troubled Chiquita Canyon landfill on Monday afternoon, prompting officials to issue advisories for nearby communities.

Texas-based Waste Connections, the operator of the landfill in Santa Clarita Valley, said in a statement that its crews were drilling a new well in the landfill when they hit a “pocket of gas about 150 feet below the ground”, said Aaron Katon, a captain with the Los Angeles county fire department.

Katon noted that the erupting cloud was not an explosion, but the production of naturally occurring gages produced by rotting material. The gas pocket carried with it “small pieces of decomposing garbage” as it expended into the air, Katon said, adding: “There was no fire, it was an escape of gas, and after that initial debris got blown off, the plume diminished significantly.”

The plume was “no hazard to anyone in the community”, Katon also said. A spokesman for the fire department told the LA Times that six landfill workers were taken to a hospital for decontamination.

The city of Santa Clarita said in a statement that residents in these areas “should be prepared to evacuate if instructed by authorities. This is a warning, not an evacuation order.”

The 639-acre garbage dump has for years wrestled to control a chain reaction within the landfill. The owners and operators are facing a state lawsuit alleging that they had mismanaged toxic waste.

The Los Angeles county department of public health later ordered the companies to immediately provide temporary hotel stays, filtered-air refuge centers, transportation assistance and air purifiers to affected residents.

LA county supervisor Kathryn Barger said in a statement that the “families of Castaic and the surrounding communities have lived with the burden of this landfill for far too long, and they should not have to wonder whether they are safe. I want answers, and I will not accept vague explanations. What happened at the site today, why it happened, and what safeguards failed are questions the operator and every responsible agency must answer fully and promptly.”

She continued: “Those responsible will be held accountable. My office will stay in close contact with our first responders and regulators, and we will share verified information with the community as soon as we have it. Residents should rely on official County sources and follow guidance from public safety officials.”

#180. ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio

US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted

There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state.

Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.

In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

Rubio’s comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, a programming language used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500, a ranking of the largest companies in the US. The researchers at US-based Calif used AI to discover the flaw and recently unearthed glitches in PHP, another computer language.

Calif said the Java flaw could allow hackers to remotely execute code, allowing them to place malicious software on a target’s systems.

The US director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, said the incidents were caused by security upgrades – such as plugging the flaws in PHP – that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.

“Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” he told the Fox Business news channel.

Tal Be’ery, a cybersecurity expert, said he did not believe the incidents were linked directly but had a common underlying theme: AI. IT systems were buckling under the pressure of adding AI or tackling flaws uncovered by AI, he said.

“Our IT infrastructure is brittle, and when AI puts massive extra pressure on it, whether through upgrades to accommodate AI or through the rapid patching that AI-driven vulnerability discovery demands,” Be’ery said.

Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which had a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eightfold – while OpenAI has also released models capable of finding previously unseen flaws. Researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw.

“[Java] is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blogpost. “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”

However, Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, said the flaw did not apply to every Java user and was specific to a library of code – Base64 – that comes bundled with a version of Java.

“It’s significant but it’s not every Java program that is affected,” he said.

In the UK the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations to keep their systems up to date, while the US and South Korean authorities also urged Java users to install security updates.

Rubio made the comments as he travelled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”. Apple also confirmed problems with its iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday but said it had resolved them.

The Democrat Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, supported the assessment that the outages were not caused by a “coordinated effort” but by attempts to shore up systems.

Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.

It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.

Before she could speak, a volunteer shouted out from the back of the hall: “Aarigaa!” Peltola picked up the refrain, and threw it right back:

“Aarigaa! Can we just chant aarigaa? Aarigaa! Aarigaa!”

It was just one word. But it encapsulated something special about Peltola and her insurgent’s campaign to unseat the incumbent Republican US senator, Dan Sullivan.

“Aarigaa” is an Iñupiaq word that is commonly understood across Alaska’s 229 federally recognised tribes. It is a word of celebration, of relief almost, that roughly translates to: “Way to go!” or “Attaboy!”

Now, Peltola genuinely has a reason for exclaiming it. On Tuesday – two weeks after the midterm elections – the tortuous count was finally completed, and she was declared winner.

In prevailing, she becomes the first Alaska Native to take a seat in the US Senate.

One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside, but India's got a massive unemployment problem. India's got a massive problem with its education system."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party responded sharply, calling him the "leader of anti-India propaganda."

Gandhi also reiterated his vote theft charge.

"140 million people who would have voted in 2024 have been removed from the electoral roll. We ask the Election Commission: how can an election be considered valid under these circumstances?" he was reported in Indian media as saying.

#173. Officials seek dismissal of lawsuit over stabbing of Ukrainian refugee on train in Charlotte

Uncle of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old who was murdered on the train, filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the city

Officials in Charlotte, North Carolina, have petitioned a judge to dismiss the wrongful death lawsuit over the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee who was killed by a man on a light rail train in the city in August 2025.

Zarutska’s uncle, Frank Scott Haskell, who was hosting Zarutska and her family in Charlotte, filed the lawsuit against the city and its transit security company, Professional Security Services, claiming that Charlotte failed to take reasonable and available safety measures to prevent her murder.

Haskell alleged in the lawsuit that the city and its security knew there were safety and crime issues related to its public transit, and they “were responsible for protecting lawful passengers from known and foreseeable dangers. Their failures caused the fatal stabbing”.

Zarutska was fatally stabbed from behind while aboard a Charlotte blue line train as she was traveling home from her shift at pizzeria. The attack, which was caught on surveillance cameras, gained international attention. Zarutska’s killing became a flashpoint in a broader public debate over violent crime, mental illness and public transit safety.

She had come to the US after living in a bomb shelter in Ukraine and had hopes of finding safety in the US. Family members described her as determined to build a safer life.

She was stabbed by suspect Decarlos Brown Jr, who was charged with first-degree murder and later deemed incompetent to stand trial. He is now in a federal medical facility to restore his competency.

Charlotte’s motion to dismiss the civil lawsuit “with prejudice” comes after mediation talks failed earlier this month.

“The City recognizes the tragic and devastating death of Iryna Zarutska as the result of an intentional criminal attack by Decarlos Brown Jr,” Charlotte’s lawyers wrote. “The City denies that it ignored passenger safety or that its conduct legally caused that attack.”

Charlotte says it “maintained an extensive security program, contracted for armed and unarmed security and company-police services, and undertook initiatives concerning public safety, security planning, training, and transit operations”.

Brown, a homeless man who once told police he was diagnosed with schizophrenia, according to the Charlotte Observer, wrote in a letter to the criminal court that he has “a body emergency. Someone has full access to my body and they are controlling me wrongfully. And law enforcement refuses to investigate it. And it requires an investigation.”

#170. Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial

Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that Letby had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Among the reasons for UCLH’s decision was that his advice to child patients relating to insulin was not considered safe. A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council, the doctors’ regulator, that the hospital could not “accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people”.

The GMC, which was already investigating Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise, subsequently applied for his registration as a doctor to be suspended. That could have resulted in his evidence in the trial of Letby – which was still in progress – being dismissed.

However, in April 2023 a medical practitioners tribunal – an independent panel that decides GMC proceedings against doctors – opted not to suspend his registration. Instead, it ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised in his work, to protect patient safety. That decision had no practical effect because UCLH had already barred him from practising at all.

While Hindmarsh’s ability to practise was being restricted, the trial of Letby continued at Manchester crown court. Her defence team was never informed that Hindmarsh’s hospital considered his professional judgment and practice so deficient as to be unsafe to child patients, or of the April 2023 tribunal ruling.

While Hindmarsh did inform Cheshire constabulary in December 2022 that he was subject to a GMC investigation, and in February 2023 the Crown Prosecution Service told Letby’s defence, her legal team was not made aware that he was later barred from practising on safety grounds.

Had they known, Letby’s defence team might have challenged his credibility as an expert witness and applied for the jury to be told or for his evidence to be dismissed.

Failures of disclosure are recognised as potential grounds for a CCRC referral and for convictions to be overturned.

The apparent lack of transparency could mean Hindmarsh breached legal rules requiring expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them any disciplinary proceedings against them and anything that may be considered to undermine their credibility. Hindmarsh declined to answer any of the Guardian’s questions about this, the hospitals’ concerns about him, or the GMC investigation.

Letby, who was a neonatal nurse at the Countess of Chester hospital, was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

She has always maintained she is innocent, and her lawyer Mark McDonald has applied to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the miscarriages of justice watchdog, to send her case back to the court of appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical experts have argued that the prosecution’s case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong, and produced reports submitted in support of her CCRC application.

Dr Shoo Lee, a renowned Canadian neonatologist who argues that the prosecution misrepresented his research, last year made public the summary findings of a 14-member expert panel he had convened. They found unanimously that the babies died or collapsed due to natural causes and poor medical care on the unit, and that there was no evidence of murders, insulin poisoning or any other deliberate harm.

Seven experts have contributed to reports submitted by McDonald to the CCRC, contesting Hindmarsh’s opinions. They argue that Hindmarsh’s calculations and diagnoses of the babies’ medical conditions were factually inaccurate in many respects, and his opinion that insulin was infused via the fluid bags is not supported by the evidence. The experts also argue that blood tests known as immunoassays, relied on by the prosecution as definitive evidence of poisoning, are known to be fallible.

Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired a two-year public inquiry after the convictions, refused to consider the experts’ arguments that Letby may have suffered a miscarriage of justice, or to wait for the CCRC decision. She produced a report in September making a series of recommendations for the NHS, on the basis that Letby was guilty.

Hindmarsh was presented to the Letby jury throughout as a distinguished authority. The lead barrister for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), Nick Johnson KC, described him to jurors as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin, in children – at UCLH from 1991, and a professor at UCL, with an eminent reputation.

When Johnson introduced Hindmarsh at the trial, he asked if he was also an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street. The jury was not told that four months earlier, in July 2022, Hindmarsh’s contract in that role at the children’s hospital had been terminated.

Hindmarsh asserted in his trial evidence that blood tests and the medical records of two babies being cared for at the Countess of Chester hospital showed they had been poisoned with insulin, most likely inserted into intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution alleged that Letby injected insulin into the bags, although there was no direct or forensic evidence that she or anybody else had done so.

Hindmarsh’s evidence alleging insulin poisoning was considered pivotal to the convictions. In summing up, the judge, James Goss, told the jury that if they were sure babies were being deliberately harmed, they could decide other babies were also being harmed, even if they were not sure about the precise cause.

Johnson presented the two cases of alleged insulin poisoning as incontrovertible evidence. The charges of attempted murder of those two babies were the first on which the jury reached guilty verdicts, and two of only three unanimous guilty verdicts.

The Guardian first revealed in March that the GMC launched an investigation into Hindmarsh on 25 November 2022, the same day he first gave evidence as an expert for the prosecution of Letby.

Great Ormond Street hospital had reported “multiple and wide-ranging concerns” to the GMC, including Hindmarsh’s “diagnosis and treatment of patients” and “cases where harm to patients has been alleged”. UCLH had been leading a formal investigation of its own into Hindmarsh, and in December 2022 it reported its similar concerns to the GMC.

Then in January 2023, while the Letby trial was still ongoing, a medical tribunal imposed orders that while the GMC investigation continued, Hindmarsh could only work at UCLH, and his clinical work had to be supervised, because otherwise he “may pose a real risk to members of the public”.

Until now, it has not been publicly known that UCLH reported further serious concerns on 15 March 2023, and informed the GMC it had excluded Hindmarsh from treating patients at all. This was less than three weeks after Hindmarsh had given his second and final day of evidence at Letby’s trial, on 24 February.

Documents seen by the Guardian show that a UCLH medical director, Dr Tim Hodgson, informed the GMC of the hospital’s decision. Hodgson wrote that Hindmarsh had breached the supervision order and given independent medical advice relating to three child patients, two involving insulin and diabetes. Hindmarsh’s medical colleagues had submitted “written concerns” about him, Hodgson said.

“On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Professor [Hindmarsh] to practice clinically even under supervision,” he wrote. “… I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

In two of the cases, Hodgson said Hindmarsh had independently advised the families that the children stop being given insulin at home. One of the children had an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a critical, life-threatening complication caused by a severe lack of insulin.

“The patient had an episode of DKA and it’s not clear whether this coincided with the alleged advice from Professor Hindmarsh,” Hodgson wrote.

In the two insulin cases, Hodgson highlighted concerns that Hindmarsh was over-focusing on rare causes of hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) and diabetes (a cause of high blood sugar). In the first case, his colleagues believed Hindmarsh was not addressing more common causes of diabetes, and in the second, that he was “not treating high glucose levels appropriately”.

Had Letby’s defence team been informed of this, it could have strengthened the case for an application to inform the jury or exclude Hindmarsh’s evidence.

Experts who have provided reports for Letby’s CCRC application have argued that Hindmarsh’s opinion that the babies were poisoned via their fluid bags was an extremely unlikely explanation for their condition. They argue that Hindmarsh failed to recognise more common, identifiable medical causes.

Hodgson also said Hindmarsh had questioned the reliability of an insulin antibodies blood test result, sharing “his concern with the family that this was an erroneous, fallible test”.

This too could have been significant to Letby’s defence. At the trial, Johnson presented results from the immunoassay blood tests as definitive and said there was “no doubt” the two babies were poisoned.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

Experts supporting Letby’s CCRC application say immunoassays are known to be fallible because they can react to antibodies in blood to give a falsely high insulin result. Hodgson’s report suggests Hindmarsh recognised that some blood tests were fallible, but he never made this clear at Letby’s trial.

The GMC responded to these new concerns by applying to the tribunal for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended. Hindmarsh’s barrister argued strongly that although he would not be treating patients because UCLH had excluded him, he should be allowed to continue working as an expert witness. Suspension, she said, would impede his ability to do so.

The barrister argued to the tribunal that Hindmarsh had not breached the supervision order and “no harm has been caused to patients”.

The three-person tribunal said it could not determine whether the previous supervision order had “technically” been breached. “However, the tribunal felt that the three cases identified by UCLH did raise concerns about patient safety,” it said.

The tribunal decided that to suspend Hindmarsh would be disproportionate and explicitly allowed him to continue working as an expert witness, saying its order should not “restrict his non-clinical work”.

Instead, it imposed a tightening of the supervision requirement so that Hindmarsh from then had to be directly supervised when treating patients. This appears to have been a theoretical measure, however, because Hindmarsh was already restricted to only working for UCLH, and the hospital had barred him from treating patients at all.

Expert witnesses have a legal duty under the criminal procedure rules to tell the party instructing them – in Hindmarsh’s case, Cheshire constabulary – anything “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. This includes any disciplinary proceedings by a regulatory body.

The rules were introduced in 2014 to improve the reliability of expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice, after a series of wrongful convictions in the late 1990s and 2000s.

Lawyers have told the Guardian that under the rules, Hindmarsh should have told the police of the April 2023 tribunal ruling and that his hospital had barred him from clinical practice.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, told the Guardian: “Whilst I cannot comment on the facts behind this complex and sensitive case, it is clear that the duty of an expert witness to make disclosure in a criminal or civil case of all material capable of undermining his opinion or detracting from his credibility is a continuous one.

“This duty extends after he has given evidence and through to the end of the proceedings. The duty continues through to any appeals, and arguably remains extant now, during the current considerations of the CCRC.

“Further restrictions imposed by a professional disciplinary tribunal on an expert’s right to practise, like those which can be imposed by the medical practitioners tribunal, are also disclosable in my view. Such restrictions are likely to be relevant to an assessment made by a jury or judge of an expert’s opinion evidence, competence and skill. For the same reasons, it also arguable that the information which led the tribunal to impose those restrictions in the first place is also disclosable.”

Lawyers have said Hindmarsh may have had a duty to tell the police and CPS initially, earlier in 2022, of the investigation into his practice led by UCLH, and that Great Ormond Street had terminated his contract. He does not appear to have done so.

When Johnson, the lead prosecutor, first introducedHindmarsh in court on 25 November 2022, he sought to clarify that the professor had an eminent position at Great Ormond Street as well as UCLH. After two questions not answered clearly, Johnson asked Hindmarsh: “Are you an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital though?” Hindmarsh replied: “Yes. At that stage, yes.”

Hindmarsh did not say his contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated four months earlier. That point was never clarified to the jury.

Hindmarsh was first informed of the GMC investigation into him on 30 November 2022. By this point, he had already made his first appearance in the Letby trial.

He told Cheshire constabulary two weeks later, on 14 December 2022. The CPS was informed two months later and told Letby’s then barrister, Ben Myers KC, on 20 February 2023, just four days before Hindmarsh was due to give his second day of evidence.

The CPS told Myers it would oppose the jury being told, because the GMC investigation into Hindmarsh had not reached a final adjudication. Myers did not then make an application to the judge for the jury to be informed.

On 23 February 2023, the day before Hindmarsh was due to return and give evidence, Johnson reminded the jury about him. “Professor Peter Hindmarsh will be here tomorrow to deal with the issue of insulin,” Johnson said. “And because he’s the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field, we will call him first.”

In July 2023, the judge referred to Hindmarsh’s evidence in his summing up. He did not mention Great Ormond Street at all, describing Hindmarsh as “emeritus professor of endocrinology at University College London and also a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at University College London hospitals”. Apparently unknown to the judge, UCLH had excluded Hindmarsh from practising as a consultant four months earlier.

Letby was convicted in August 2023. The GMC investigation into Hindmarsh never reached a final determination. In November 2024 Hindmarsh applied to remove himself from registration as a doctor. The GMC allowed this, a process known as “voluntary erasure”, which meant the investigation was stopped with no final adjudication.

The CPS has confirmed to the Guardian that it did not disclose to the defence anything relating to Hindmarsh being barred from clinical practice or the April 2023 tribunal ruling, because it had not been made aware of it.

Cheshire constabulary declined to provide information to the Guardian, so it is not clear whether Hindmarsh did or did not tell the police. Either way, it was not passed to the CPS, which would have disclosed it to Letby’s defence.

“Cheshire constabulary will not be commenting further in relation to this case,” a spokesperson said.

A CPS spokesperson said: “The CPS met all its disclosure obligations and no objections were raised by the defence at any stage in relation to expert evidence relied on by the prosecution.”

The CPS’ statement is made on the basis that it disclosed what it knew to the defence, and it had not been told about the tribunal ruling or that Hindmarsh was barred from treating patients. Johnson’s representatives did not reply to questions from the Guardian.

McDonald, Letby’s lawyer, said: “Peter Hindmarsh’s evidence was pivotal to the prosecution’s case against Lucy Letby. The insulin allegations were not simply another part of the prosecution’s case; they were its cornerstone, presented as scientific proof that she had deliberately poisoned babies and was capable of murder.

“It shaped the jury’s perception of Lucy and provided the lens through which they were invited to view every other allegation. This was not evidence that could be neatly confined to two convictions. Its influence permeated the entire trial. If the foundations of the insulin cases are unsafe, the consequences for the safety of the wider convictions cannot be overstated.”

The Guardian asked Hindmarsh detailed questions about the hospitals’ concerns, UCLH excluding him from clinical practice, and the GMC investigation, and put to him that he appeared not to have made adequate disclosure under the criminal procedure rules.

A representative for Hindmarsh replied: “He has no comment in relation to these questions and points.”

#168. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#166. Ministers to drop foie gras imports ban to help seal EU food trade deal

Animal welfare charities criticise ‘backwards step’ on foie gras, production of which has been banned in UK since 2007

Ministers will drop plans to ban foie gras imports into the UK in order to smooth a trade deal with the EU that will be announced this week.

As first reported by the Financial Times, the proposed ban will be officially dropped on Friday when the government announces its sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) trade deal with the EU to reduce checks and paperwork on imports and exports of food and drink with the bloc.

Labour promised before coming to power that it would ban foie gras imports. Before the election, Steve Reed, the then shadow environment secretary, said Labour would “ban the commercial import of foie gras, where ducks and geese are aggressively force-fed”. He labelled the practice “beyond disgusting”.

Foie gras is made by force-feeding ducks and geese grain through a funnel or tube that has been thrust down the bird’s neck – a process known as gavage that swells the animal’s liver to many times its normal size. The livers are then harvested.

Banning it has proved difficult as EU countries including France produce and export the product and are against other members putting in place an import ban. The Guardian reported earlier this year that ministers were preparing to drop the ban in order to secure concessions.

Sustainability chefs and animal welfare charities have criticised the U-turn. Boris Johnson’s government promised to use the powers granted by Brexit to ban the “cruel” product, which still appears on menus across the country almost seven years after the UK officially left the EU.

Some restaurants still sell foie gras but many shops have removed it from sale, including the king’s grocer, Fortnum & Mason, which took it off shelves in 2021. The production of foie gras has been banned in the UK since 2007.

The French chef Alexis Gauthier used to sell more foie gras than any other restaurant in London before converting to a vegan diet and menu. He now sells a mushroom-based “faux gras” to customers of his Soho restaurant, who include the former Beatle Paul McCartney. Gauthier said the ban being dropped was “terrible news”.

“I find it very sad our government capitulates so easily,” he said. “The cruelty of foie gras belongs firmly in the history books, not in a progressive society in 2026.”

Will Murray, a co-founder of the sustainable British restaurant Fallow, also based in London, serves a mushroom parfait rather than foie gras. He said: “This feels like a step in the wrong direction with regards to animal welfare. I think London diners aren’t really asking for a big return of foie gras on menus.”

David Bowles, the head of public affairs at the RSPCA, said: “We are extremely disappointed that farm animal welfare laws have been put on the chopping block as part of this new deal. Any suggestions plans to act on foie gras are being shelved to ease EU realignment are deeply concerning for animals and would be a clear backwards step.”

A spokesperson for the charity Four Paws said: “The UK prohibited the production of foie gras nearly 20 years ago because of the serious animal welfare concerns associated with force-feeding ducks and geese. Yet foie gras produced using these same methods can still be imported and sold here. As the UK strengthens its relationship with the EU, animal welfare must not become a casualty of closer trade ties.”

Government insiders indicated that the ban would be dropped but noted that the method of production was banned in the UK. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the method raises welfare concerns.

They said: “We are negotiating a food and drink deal that will slash red tape and costly paperwork, make it easier and cheaper to export seafood, boost the British economy by up to £5bn a year, and back British businesses and jobs. We are working closely with businesses to ensure a smooth transition so they can make the most of the benefits this deal unlocks.”

#163. UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds

Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment regulator says

Environment secretary Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the catastrophic decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.

New data shows wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

In the last five decades, Britain has lost more than 73 million wild birds from its landscape, according to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO).

The loss of wild birds includes some of Britain’s best-loved garden birds, including swifts, turtledoves and tree sparrows, as well as wood warblers and bullfinches.

Ministers have legal responsibilities to take action to recover bird populations to healthy levels, as well as specific duties to designate Special Protection Areas (SPAs) where birds and their habitats are legally protected.

But the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP), the independent environmental regulator, said on Wednesday that the environment secretary, her department and Natural England were all breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds.

Eagle has breached environmental law by failing to classify new SPAs, extend existing sites or add new species to those that are protected, the regulator said.

Natural England is in breach of environmental law, according to the OEP, by failing to take the action needed to maintain or restore wild bird populations to appropriate levels and ensure they have sufficient habitats.

The government’s independent nature adviser is also accused of breaching the law by failing to carry out a review of whether there is sufficient habitat for wild birds.

The OEP said the review was important because it was supposed to provide an expert and independent assessment of whether there is sufficient diversity and area of habitat for wild birds, as well as to identify gaps and explain what action is needed to support their recovery.

The continued decline in bird populations comes despite evidence that the public’s interest and attention to wild birds is growing. In May, the RSPB reported a 47% increase in the number of people enjoying bird watching over the past eight years.

Helen Venn, chief regulatory officer for the OEP, said there have been continued delays by ministers to protect bird populations.

“As a nation of bird-lovers, and with birds acting as important indicators for the state of our nature more widely, the latest statistics showing declines in the populations of some of our most treasured species are deeply concerning,” said Venn.

“This is why it is important that Defra and Natural England do carry out their legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

“Continued delay has left a significant number of sites for wild bird populations without the levels of protection they need and allowed the scale of the actions needed to deliver a sufficient SPA network to build up.”

There are 82 SPAs in England, as well as six cross-border and offshore sites.

The government is legally bound to expand and increase protected areas across the country as part of its 30 by 30 commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature’s recovery by 2030.

But despite repeated promises by Labour’s environment ministers, wild bird populations across the UK are showing no sign of widespread recovery, with both short and long-term trends indicating that nearly half of all species are in decline, according to Defra’s latest statistics.

Beccy Speight, the RSPB’s chief executive, said: “We now expect urgent action, including the designation of new and extended Special Protection Areas and other targeted measures for species such as curlew, bittern and hen harrier, which are in most need. Successive governments right across the UK have known about these problems for years. The time for navel gazing has long passed; the time for taking action is now, before it is too late.”

The Department for Environment was approached for comment.

Germany's governing coalition has agreed to reduce electricity tax for households and businesses.

The cut will lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level.

The agreement between Chancelor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and his junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), was reached after multiple failed attempts.

Funding for the tax cut has only been secured for the year 2027, but the coalition stressed in a summary document of the agreement that it aimed to achieve a "permanent reduction." An extension is contingent on finding a way to fund it into 2028, according to the paper.

The coalition partners said that the tax cut will be funded by surplus funds from subsidies under the renewable energy bill, as the government anticipates lower demand for renewable energy subsidies next year.

The government is also to introduce a three-month cap on fuel prices in January.

The CDU/CSU and SPD promised in their 2025 coalition deal to cut taxes for all consumers, but initially only applied a reduction for industry, agriculture and forestry. Wednesday's agreement extends cuts to households and to businesses that did not qualify for the initial reduction.

Germany has some of the highest electricity prices in Europe, in part thanks to shocks following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and by the United States and Israel's war with Iran.
